extracted.intended_audience: students, researchers and practitioners of intellectual property/patent law (especially those studying inventive step at EPO and USPTO)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and case-based analysis for assessing inventive step (non‑obviousness) in patent applications before the European Patent Office and the United States Patent and Trademark Office, focusing on characteristics of the skilled person, methodologies (problem-solution, Graham/TSM), evidentiary indicia and case law.

rubrics_metrics.name: EPC patentability prerequisites
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the EPC (Art. 52(1) and related provisions) an invention must be new, involve an inventive step and be susceptible of industrial application to be granted a patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Art. 56 EPC states: 'An invention shall be considered as involving an inventive step if, having regard to the state of the art, it is not obvious to a person skilled in the art.' Technical character is required; technical progress/useful effect is not a strictly required separate test under EPC.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of 'obvious' (EPO perspective)
rubrics_metrics.description: Obvious means something that 'does not go beyond the normal progress of technology but merely follows logically from the prior art' and 'does neither involve an inventive activity nor involve the exercise of any ability beyond that to be expected of PSA.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assessment focuses on whether claimed subject‑matter goes beyond what PSA would do as a logical next step from the prior art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Person Skilled in the Art (PSA) characteristics
rubrics_metrics.description: PSA should be presumed to be an ordinary practitioner in a field of technology aware of what was common general knowledge at the priority date, with access to everything in the state of the art and normal means for routine work and experimentation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PSA may represent a group (e.g., research or production team). PSA is an expert but 'not possessed of any inventive or creativity capability' and is 'devoid of mental or practical effort, or purposive selection, when trying to find a solution.' PSA is assumed to act with a specific technical purpose, not idle curiosity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Temporal anchoring of PSA/PHOSITA
rubrics_metrics.description: The characteristics of the person skilled in the art (PSA/PHOSITA) must be assessed at the time of the invention (priority date).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because the invention date can be several years earlier, reconstructing PSA skills at that time is difficult and affects objectivity of the assessment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Problem‑solution approach (overview)
rubrics_metrics.description: EPO's problem-solution approach is used to assess inventive step objectively and to avoid hindsight: (A) determine state of the art and closest prior art; (B) establish the objective technical problem; (C) consider whether the prior art would have prompted PSA to modify the closest prior art to arrive at the claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Derived from Rule 42(1)(c) EPC; requires formulating distinguishing features, then an objectively framed technical problem that does not anticipate the solution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Step A — determine closest prior art / state of the art
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine the state of the art including neighbouring fields and then identify the closest prior art which corresponds to a similar use and requires minimal structural/functional modifications to arrive at the claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Closest prior art selection can be replaced by a 'reasonable selection' of prior art; examiners should consider relevant neighbouring fields where the same or similar problems arise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Step B — establish objective technical problem
rubrics_metrics.description: Formulate the objective technical problem by studying the application and closest prior art, identifying the distinguishing features, and stating the task of modifying the closest prior art to provide the technical effects the invention provides.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The technical problem should be formulated so as not to anticipate the solution; it need not be the problem expressly stated by the applicant and need not be an improvement over prior art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Step C — evaluate whether prior art would prompt modification
rubrics_metrics.description: Starting from the closest prior art and the objective technical problem, consider whether any teaching in the prior art would obviously have prompted PSA before the priority date to modify the closest prior art so as to arrive at the claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This step tests whether a skilled person would have been led to the claimed combination without ex‑post knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combination inventions — synergy vs aggregation
rubrics_metrics.description: A combination claim may involve an inventive step if the functional interaction between features achieves a synergistic effect; if the claim is merely an aggregation of individually obvious features with no greater synergistic effect, there is no inventive step.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider whether the prior art suggested precisely the claimed combination. If it was 'obvious to try' but there was no reasonable expectation of success, the invention may still be inventive. 'Reasonable expectation of success' is distinct from mere hope.

rubrics_metrics.name: Secondary indicia (EPO guidance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Where objective evaluation of prior art teachings does not provide a clear picture, examiners may investigate secondary indications of inventive step such as long‑felt need, inactivity of the art, or commercial success.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Secondary indicia are not a substitute for technical assessment. Commercial success must be immediate, linked to features of the invention, and not explained by external factors (marketing, sales techniques). Long-felt need must be demonstrable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Problem‑solution approach is not mandatory
rubrics_metrics.description: TBA case law (1994) states the problem-solution approach is 'no more than one possible route for the assessment of inventiveness.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners/boards need not be tied to a single closest prior art and may use a reasonable selection of prior art to avoid procedural rigidity; alternative lines of attack/defence are permitted under procedural principles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoiding hindsight / ex‑post analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Correct use of the problem‑and‑solution approach rules out ex‑post facto analysis which inadmissibly makes use of knowledge of the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A difficulty arises where the same examiner formulates the problem and assesses inventive step; scrutiny is required to ensure the problem formulation does not incorporate knowledge of the solution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assessment of obvious‑to‑try and reasonable expectation of success
rubrics_metrics.description: When a combination or modification was 'obvious to try', the presence or absence of a 'reasonable expectation of success' is a key factor in deciding inventive step.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A reasonable expectation of success should not be equated with an understandable hope; contemporaneous activity in the area (others working on it) may suggest obviousness to try but does not necessarily demonstrate reasonable expectation of success.

rubrics_metrics.name: Common general knowledge and neighbouring fields
rubrics_metrics.description: PSA is presumed aware of common general knowledge and relevant teachings in neighbouring technical fields where similar problems arise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPO guidance directs inclusion of neighbouring-field art in the state of the art; however, Boards often focus on a precise hint in the prior art — common general knowledge is sometimes under‑emphasised in practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidentiary standard for commercial success as secondary consideration
rubrics_metrics.description: Commercial success can be used as secondary evidence of inventive step only if (i) success is immediate, (ii) success is derived from the features of the invention, and (iii) success is not due to other influences (marketing, advertising).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claimants must provide evidence connecting sales/performance to claimed technical features; mere market success without link is insufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: USPTO / US law markers: PHOSITA, Graham factors and TSM
rubrics_metrics.description: United States analysis relies on the Person Having Ordinary Skill in the Art (PHOSITA), the Graham factual inquiries (e.g., scope/contents of prior art, differences, level of ordinary skill, secondary considerations), and the TSM (Teaching, Suggestion, Motivation) test as a tool for finding motivation to combine prior art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: After KSR, courts endorsed a more flexible approach to motivation to combine (TSM not rigid); common sense and ordinary creativity can play a greater role in obviousness analyses at USPTO/US courts.

rubrics_metrics.name: KSR flexible standard and its effects
rubrics_metrics.description: KSR v. Teleflex emphasizes a more flexible obviousness inquiry, permitting combinations based on 'ordinary creativity,' common sense, and broader consideration of common general knowledge — aimed at reducing patent over‑issuance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: KSR decreases reliance on rigid formalistic tests and increases inquiry into whether a skilled artisan would have combined references with a reasonable expectation of success.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of Examiner/Board explanation about PSA/PHOSITA
rubrics_metrics.description: When reversing an Examiner's decision for lack of inventive step, Boards frequently state that the Examiner 'has not clearly explained how PSA/PHOSITA would have an incentive to combine the teachings of the prior art' but often do not elaborate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Boards should provide detailed reasoning about the skills and incentives of PSA/PHOSITA; failure to do so contributes to subjectivity and unpredictability in the inventive step assessment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection and use of prior art (reasonable selection principle)
rubrics_metrics.description: It is not always necessary to determine a single closest prior art if there is a reasonable selection of prior art; being tied to one selected closest prior art could prevent consideration of alternative possibilities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examining Departments and Boards may replace a chosen closest prior art with other reasonable prior art; investigation should avoid artificially formulated problems and normally start from the technical problem identified in the patent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical constraints influencing objectivity (procedural/design issues)
rubrics_metrics.description: Factors that influence objectivity include examiner skills, hindsight knowledge, examination guidelines, difficulty in defining the fictive skilled person, and the fact that examiners/boards decide without the physical product in hand.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Procedural reforms (e.g., separating the examiner who frames the problem from the one who assesses obviousness) or shortening exclusivity have been suggested to improve assessment objectivity, but such proposals raise further practical issues.
